payload.name: aluminum
payload.structure_source: fcc Al, ase.build.bulk, lattice relaxed with MACE-MP-0 medium
payload.rationale: Melting point of Al at ambient pressure via solid-liquid coexistence MD with MACE-MP-0; Cu validation against ITS-90 fixed point.

_fulfilled_need.query: Find the melting point of aluminum at ambient pressure.

method.engine: ASE 3 + mace-torch (cuEquivariance, float32) on NVIDIA GB10
method.protocol: Solid-liquid coexistence (interface direction) method. 4x4x8 fcc supercell (512 atoms) from MACE-relaxed a0=4.039 A; solid equilibrated by anisotropic Berendsen NPT at 900 K (1.5 ps); top half melted with Langevin at 2250 K (2 ps) while bottom half fixed, then 0.5 ps at 900 K; coexistence runs at 825/900/975/1050 K with anisotropic Berendsen NPT (P=0, taut=100 fs, taup=500 fs), 7 ps each. Phase growth judged from potential-energy drift (fit t>1 ps) and final fraction of 12-coordinated atoms. Results: 825 K slope -0.0094 eV/atom/ps, CN12 fraction 0.65 (crystal grows); 900 K +0.0026, 0.19 (melts); 975 K +0.0086, 0.04 (melts); 1050 K +0.0070, 0.04 (melts). Tm bracketed in (825, 900) K; reported value = bracket midpoint, uncertainty = half-width.

payload.note: PREMISE: Tm is well-defined and accessible with an MLIP by two-phase coexistence (avoids the superheating of single-phase heating); 512 atoms and 7 ps are enough to see the interface move at |T-Tm| >~ 40 K but not to resolve Tm more finely. VALIDATION (same model, cell shape, protocol, run length): Cu, independent ITS-90 fixed point 1357.77 K (tier1.json, NIST): crystal grew at 1200 and 1300 K, melted at 1400 and 1500 K -> MACE-MP-0 Tm(Cu) in (1300,1400) K, consistent with experiment. RESULT: MACE-MP-0 Tm(Al) in (825, 900) K; linear interpolation of the energy-drift zero gives ~884 K, inside the bracket. The measured Al melting point is 933.45 K (NIST-JANAF, tier1.json), i.e. this model predicts a melting point roughly 35-110 K too low (~4-12%); the experimental value lies outside the simulated bracket, so the discrepancy is attributed to the potential (PBE-trained foundation model, not fit to Al liquid thermodynamics), not to sampling. For the physical answer use 933.45 K; this number is the MACE-MP-0 prediction. UNCERTAINTY (+/-38 K) covers only the temperature-grid bracketing resolution; it does NOT cover the model (DFT/MLIP) error, finite-size effects (512 atoms, ~16 A interfaces separation), Berendsen barostat artefacts, float32 precision, or stochastic interface fluctuations (one run per T). The 900 K run had only a small positive drift, so Tm(MACE) is probably in the upper part of the bracket (~870-895 K).

method.engine: none for the reported value (measured reference); MLIP cross-check from parent result: ASE 3 + mace-torch on NVIDIA GB10
method.model: Experiment: NIST-JANAF Thermochemical Tables, Al (https://janaf.nist.gov/tables/Al-001.txt, 'CRYSTAL <--> LIQUID' at 933.450 K), as recorded in /data/calibration/tier1.json. Simulation cross-check: MACE-MP-0 medium (PBE/MPtrj foundation MLIP)
method.protocol: Reported value = measured melting point of Al at ambient pressure (1 bar), taken from NIST-JANAF via tier1.json. No new simulation was run for this rerun. The parent MACE-MP-0 two-phase coexistence run (512 atoms, 4x4x8 fcc, anisotropic Berendsen NPT, 825/900/975/1050 K, 7 ps each, one run per T) bracketed the model's Tm in (825, 900) K. That run did not recover the measured value, so it fails validation for Al and is kept only as a documented model cross-check, not as the answer.

payload.note: RERUN after checker 'disagree' (b0465de9). I agree with the checker. The parent result's 862 +/- 38 K is a MACE-MP-0 prediction, not the melting point of aluminum. The measured value lies outside its bracket, and its error bar covered only the temperature-grid spacing. CORRECTED ANSWER: Tm(Al, 1 bar) = 933.45 K (NIST-JANAF). The ITS-90 freezing point of Al, 933.473 K, agrees within 0.03 K (tier1.json marks the copy it saw as unofficial). The +/-0.1 K uncertainty covers JANAF rounding and the JANAF vs ITS-90 difference; the 1 bar vs 1 atm difference is negligible (dTm/dP is about 6-7 K/GPa, so about 0.001 K). PREMISE: well posed. Al has a sharp first-order melting transition at ambient pressure, and the property is measured directly to mK precision. VALIDATION: the reported number is itself the independent measured reference, so no simulation validation applies to it. The MLIP route was tested and FAILED for Al. MACE-MP-0 (same protocol that bracketed Cu at 1300-1400 K, vs 1357.77 K measured) gives Tm(Al) in (825, 900) K, about 35-110 K (4-12%) below experiment. This fits the known tendency of PBE-level models to underestimate Al's Tm. Even as a model number it is weakly constrained: one seed per T, a small 512-atom cell, and the 900 K upper bound rests on a weak drift (+0.0026 eV/atom/ps, final CN12 fraction 0.19) that a second seed could flip. A defensible MACE-MP-0 statement is Tm ~ 860-900 K, with an additional model bias of about -50 to -110 K relative to experiment. Do not use the MLIP number as the Al melting point. Getting a simulation-based value within about 20 K of experiment would need an Al-specific potential validated on liquid thermodynamics (or fine-tuning MACE on Al solid+liquid data), larger cells (>=2000 atoms), several seeds per T and finer temperature steps near Tm.
